rows.branch: All branches (the Four Books are held by the Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools and by modern New Confucians alike)
rows.reference: Mencius 7A.33 (ctext: Jin Xin I, 33; Legge VII.A.33)
rows.original: 殺一無罪非仁也，非其有而取之非義也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Asked what a scholar's aim is, Mencius answers: humaneness and rightness, nothing more. To kill even one person who has done no wrong is not humane; to take what is not yours is not right.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit. Killing anyone without guilt is against humaneness, with no limit by status, sex, age or faith, so it reaches newborns, wives, servants and strangers (rules 7 and 9). It names the innocent only; for the guilty acting on private authority see Mencius 2B.8. K0: covers every innocent victim whatever the motive. Would decide 'taught' once verified (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: the shared web search budget for this turn was exhausted before any search ran, and direct page fetches fail here (DNS error on ctext.org and zh.wikisource.org); text recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/jin-xin-i.

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.2 (ctext: Gong Sun Chou I, 2; Legge II.A.2, near the end of the chapter)
rows.original: 行一不義，殺一不辜而得天下，皆不為也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased from the Chinese
rows.says: Comparing Confucius with the sages Bo Yi and Yi Yin, Mencius says what they share: each, given a small state, could have won the whole realm, but none would have done one wrong act or killed one innocent person to gain it.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit that the tradition's highest models would not kill one innocent person even for the greatest possible gain; reaches every innocent (rule 7). K0: Explicit for killing for gain. Would decide once verified (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted before any search ran; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/gong-sun-chou-i.

rows.reference: Mencius 2B.8 (ctext: Gong Sun Chou II, 8; Legge II.B.8)
rows.original: 孰可以殺之？…為士師，則可以殺之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased from the Chinese
rows.says: Asked whether he urged Qi to attack Yan, Mencius uses a comparison. If someone asked whether a murderer may be put to death, he would say yes; if asked who may put him to death, he would say: the chief criminal judge. In the same way only a ruler appointed by Heaven may attack a state.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Clear teaching that even a person guilty of murder may be killed only by the appointed judge, not by anyone acting on their own authority. This is the reach K1 needs for 'the wicked' and K0 needs for revenge (rule 5). The judge's killing is context (exclusion (a)) and the attack on Yan is war (exclusion (b)). Rated Clear teaching, not Explicit, because the point is an analogy inside an argument about war.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/gong-sun-chou-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 7B.31 (ctext: Jin Xin II, 31; Legge VII.B.31)
rows.original: 人能充無欲害人之心，而仁不可勝用也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased from the Chinese
rows.says: Everyone has things they cannot bear to do; extending this to what they can bear is humaneness. If a person fills out the heart that does not wish to harm others, their humaneness will be more than they can use.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: wider rule (METHOD section 3; rule 7). The heart that does not want to harm anyone is the root of humaneness and is owed to everyone. Clear teaching rather than Explicit because it is framed as self-cultivation, not as a rule.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/jin-xin-ii.

rows.reference: Analects 15.24 (Legge XV.23) and 12.2 (Legge XII.2)
rows.original: 己所不欲，勿施於人
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893)
rows.says: What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others. Confucius gives it as the one word to live by (15.24) and as part of humaneness (12.2).
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: wider rule (rule 7), as already accepted for L1 in Article I's households annex: no one wants to be killed, and the rule reaches everyone. On its own it neither marks the self-defence exception nor addresses rulers' punishments (context, rule 5). These are the only counted rows for K1 and K0 that are verified so far.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule; the rule itself is Explicit)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's earlier research (Article I rows 6a and 6b; 12.2 also at ctext.org/analects/yan-yuan); not re-searched in this run.

rows.branch: All branches (the Lu-Wang school reads the Great Learning in the older text order, but the passage is in both)
rows.reference: Great Learning, commentary ch. 10 (Zhu Xi's arrangement)
rows.original: 所惡於上，毋以使下 … 此之謂絜矩之道
rows.translation: James Legge (1861)
rows.says: What you dislike from those above you, do not do to those below you, and so in every direction: this is the way of the measuring square.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: wider rule (rule 7) addressed to anyone with power over others, which matters for the masters, parents and husbands K1 binds. Same limits as Analects 15.24.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's earlier research (Article I row 6c); not re-searched in this run.

rows.reference: Analects 12.22 (Legge XII.22); Mencius 4B.28 (ctext: Li Lou II, 28; Legge IV.B.28)
rows.original: 樊遲問仁。子曰：「愛人。」 ; 仁者愛人
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked what humaneness is, Confucius says: love people. Mencius repeats that the humane person loves others.
rows.bearing: Supports K1 by implication. Rated Implied because it states an attitude, not a rule of conduct, and the same texts accept a ruler's punishments. Not needed for the label.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/analects/yan-yuan and ctext.org/mengzi/li-lou-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.6 (ctext: Gong Sun Chou I, 6; Legge II.A.6)
rows.original: 今人乍見孺子將入於井，皆有怵惕惻隱之心
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Everyone has a heart that cannot bear others' suffering: anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, not for gain or praise. Whoever lacks this heart is not human.
rows.bearing: K1 (rule 9): Implied. It shows that compassion is owed to any small child, not only one's own, but it describes a feeling rather than teaching a rule against killing.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/gong-sun-chou-i.

rows.reference: Mencius 5B.4 (ctext: Wan Zhang II, 4; Legge V.B.4), quoting the Announcement to Kang (Kang Gao) of the Classic of Documents
rows.original: 殺越人于貨，閔不畏死，凡民罔不譈
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius quotes the Documents with approval: people who kill others to seize their goods, reckless and unafraid of death, are hated by all the people. Such men, he says, may be put to death without first waiting to teach them.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching that killing for gain is among the worst wrongs, given by Mencius through an approved quotation. The execution of such killers is court context (rule 5).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/wan-zhang-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 3B.5 (ctext: Teng Wen Gong II, 5; Legge III.B.5)
rows.original: 有童子以黍肉餉，殺而奪之 … 為匹夫匹婦復讎也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: The lord of Ge and his men robbed those carrying food to the fields and killed those who would not hand it over; they killed a boy bringing millet and meat and took it. King Tang attacked Ge because of that boy, and everyone said he did it not to enrich himself but to avenge ordinary men and women.
rows.bearing: K0 and K1: Clear teaching, through a story Mencius approves, that killing even a child to take his food is a grave wrong. Tang's 'revenge' is a punitive war by a ruler (rule 5, exclusion (b)), not private revenge. K3 context: the same chapter says Tang's campaigns punished rulers and comforted their people.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/teng-wen-gong-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 5A.2 and 5A.3 (ctext: Wan Zhang I, 2 and 3; Legge V.A.2 and V.A.3)
rows.original: 仁人之於弟也，不藏怒焉，不宿怨焉，親愛之而已矣
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Shun's father and his half-brother Xiang tried to kill him (setting fire to a granary he was repairing, filling in a well he was digging). When Shun became ruler he did not punish Xiang but gave him a fief, kept at a distance. Mencius explains: a humane man does not store up anger or nurse resentment against his brother; he simply loves him.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching, through the model ruler, that one does not take revenge even on someone who tried to kill you. Its stated reason concerns a brother, so alone it reaches family; with the Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 and Mencius 2B.8 it covers anyone. Shun's punishment of other offenders as ruler (5A.3) is court context (rule 5).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/wan-zhang-i.

rows.reference: Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 10 (Zhu Xi's arrangement; Zhong Yong chapter of the Book of Rites)
rows.original: 寬柔以教，不報無道，南方之強也，君子居之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked about strength, Confucius contrasts the southern kind (teaching with patience and gentleness, not repaying unreasonable treatment), which the noble person keeps to, with the northern kind (sleeping on weapons and armour, dying without regret), which the forceful keep to; he then praises a strength that holds to the mean.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching that the noble person does not retaliate against wrongs done to him, which reaches revenge killing. Zhu Xi is recalled as glossing 不報無道 as taking an outrage without repaying it (not verified in this run). Treated as primary, so it may stand alone (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/liji/zhong-yong.

rows.reference: Analects 16.7 and 16.10 (Legge XVI.7 and XVI.10)
rows.original: 血氣方剛，戒之在鬥 … 忿思難，見得思義
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: 16.7: in the prime of life, when the blood is strong, the noble person guards against fighting. 16.10: when angry, he thinks of the trouble anger may bring; when he sees a chance of gain, he thinks of what is right.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching as a wider rule (rule 7): restrain anger and fighting, and test every gain by rightness. Neither passage names killing, so each counts only as a wider rule that includes killing in anger or for gain.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/analects/ji-shi.

rows.reference: Analects 12.21 and 12.10 (Legge XII.21 and XII.10)
rows.original: 一朝之忿，忘其身，以及其親，非惑與 ; 愛之欲其生，惡之欲其死…是惑也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: 12.21: to forget yourself, and endanger your parents, in one morning's anger is delusion. 12.10: to want someone to live when you love them and to die when you hate them is confusion.
rows.bearing: K0: 12.21 is Clear teaching against acting on sudden anger (commentators read it of fighting that brings ruin on oneself and one's family), as a wider rule. 12.10 treats wishing death on someone you hate as confusion; Implied as to killing.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/analects/yan-yuan.

rows.reference: Mencius 7B.7 (ctext: Jin Xin II, 7; Legge VII.B.7)
rows.original: 殺人之父，人亦殺其父；殺人之兄，人亦殺其兄
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius: now I know how grave it is to kill a man's kin. Kill a man's father and he will kill yours; kill his elder brother and he will kill yours. Then you have all but killed them yourself, with only one step between.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching against killing others' kin, given as a warning. It presupposes that sons and brothers take revenge, without approving or condemning the avenger (rule 4: Implied, does not decide).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/jin-xin-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 7A.35 (ctext: Jin Xin I, 35; Legge VII.A.35)
rows.original: 瞽瞍殺人，則如之何？…執之而已矣 … 竊負而逃
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked what would happen if Shun's father killed a man while Shun ruled and Gao Yao was judge, Mencius says Gao Yao would simply arrest him and Shun could not forbid it. Shun would throw away the realm like an old sandal, carry his father off in secret and live happily by the sea.
rows.bearing: Limits enforcement, not the rule. The killing is a crime even for the ruler's father, and the judge's arrest is right. The son's flight with the killer shows the tension between family loyalty and justice, which is court context (rule 5). Does not contradict K1 or K0.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/jin-xin-i.

rows.reference: Analects 14.34 (Legge XIV.36)
rows.original: 以德報怨，何如？…以直報怨，以德報德
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked about repaying injury with kindness, Confucius asks what would then repay kindness: repay injury with uprightness, and kindness with kindness.
rows.bearing: Limits a duty to forgive, not the bar on killing. 直 is a straight, fair response, not revenge; Zhu Xi is recalled as glossing it as complete impartiality (至公而無私; not verified in this run). No classical reading found takes it to allow killing. Recorded as counter-evidence considered; does not contradict K0.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/analects/xian-wen.

rows.reference: Analects 12.19 and 13.11 (Legge XII.19 and XIII.11)
rows.original: 子為政，焉用殺？ ; 善人為邦百年，亦可以勝殘去殺矣
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: 12.19: Ji Kangzi asks about killing the lawless to help the law-abiding; Confucius asks why one who governs should use killing at all: desire the good and the people will be good. 13.11: good people governing a state for a hundred years could overcome cruelty and do away with killing.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5, exclusion (a)): a ruler's punishments. Shows the tradition's reluctance even about lawful killing; does not decide.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/analects/yan-yuan and ctext.org/analects/zi-lu.

rows.reference: Analects 20.2 (Legge XX.2)
rows.original: 不教而殺謂之虐
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893); paraphrased
rows.says: Among four evils of government, to put people to death without first teaching them is cruelty.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5): rulers' punishments.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's earlier research (households annex row CO-2); not re-searched in this run.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.7 (ctext: Liang Hui Wang II, 7; Legge I.B.7) and 4B.4 (ctext: Li Lou II, 4; Legge IV.B.4)
rows.original: 國人皆曰可殺，然後察之；見可殺焉，然後殺之 ; 無罪而殺士，則大夫可以去
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: 1B.7: a ruler should not execute anyone because his attendants or great officers say so; only when the whole people say so should he examine the case, and execute only if he finds the person deserves it. 4B.4: if scholars are put to death without crime, officers may leave the state; if the people are slaughtered without crime, scholars may move away.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5). Shows that even a ruler may not kill without proven guilt.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-ii and ctext.org/mengzi/li-lou-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.5 (ctext: Liang Hui Wang II, 5; Legge I.B.5), with Zhu Xi's commentary
rows.original: 罪人不孥 ; Zhu Xi: 惡惡止其身，不及妻子也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Under King Wen's government, offenders' wives and children were not punished with them. Zhu Xi: hatred of wrongdoing stops at the offender's own person.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5): a ruler's punishments. Bears on K1 by implication: family members are not to suffer for another's offence.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's earlier research (households annex row CO-3); not re-searched in this run.

rows.reference: Mencius 1A.4 (ctext: Liang Hui Wang I, 4; Legge I.A.4), with 1A.3
rows.original: 殺人以梃與刃，有以異乎？…以刃與政，有以異乎？ ; 始作俑者，其無後乎
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius gets King Hui to agree that killing a man with a club, with a blade or by misgovernment is no different. He cites Confucius cursing the first maker of human figures for burial because they imitated people; how much worse to let people starve. (1A.3: blaming the harvest for deaths is like stabbing a man and blaming the weapon.)
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5): addressed to a ruler. For K1 it is Implied evidence that causing death by policy counts as killing, and that even an image of burying people with the dead was condemned.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory (the households annex research also left 1A.4 unverified). Check at ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-i.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.11 (ctext: Liang Hui Wang II, 11; Legge I.B.11)
rows.original: 若殺其父兄，係累其子弟，毀其宗廟，遷其重器，如之何其可也？…反其旄倪
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: After Qi took Yan, Mencius told King Xuan: the people of Yan welcomed your army with food and drink, hoping to be saved; if you kill their fathers and elder brothers, bind their sons and younger brothers, destroy their ancestral temples and carry off their treasures, how can that be right? Send back the old and the young you have taken, and leave once a ruler is set up.
rows.bearing: War: context for K1 (rule 5, exclusion (b)). K3: Clear teaching against killing and capturing the people of a conquered state, with the old and the young named.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory (also unverified in the households annex research). Check at ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 7B.4 and 7B.3 (ctext: Jin Xin II, 4 and 3; Legge VII.B.4 and VII.B.3)
rows.original: 無畏！寧爾也，非敵百姓也 ; 以至仁伐至不仁，而何其血之流杵也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: 7B.4: those who boast of skill in battle are great criminals; when King Wu attacked Shang he told its people: do not fear, I come to give you peace, I am not the enemy of the people. 7B.3: it would be better to have no Book of Documents than to believe all of it; Mencius accepts only two or three strips of its Wu Cheng chapter, for when the most humane attacks the most inhumane, how could blood flow enough to float pestles?
rows.bearing: K3: Clear teaching that the people of an enemy state are not the enemy, and that a humane war does not slaughter. 7B.3 also shows Mencius refusing to believe a classic's report of mass killing because it conflicts with humaneness, a reconciling method of the tradition's own. War context for K1 (rule 5).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/jin-xin-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 4A.14 (ctext: Li Lou I, 14; Legge IV.A.14), 6B.8 (ctext: Gaozi II, 8; Legge VI.B.8), 7B.2 (Legge VII.B.2) and 1A.6 (Legge I.A.6)
rows.original: 爭地以戰，殺人盈野…罪不容於死 ; 況於殺人以求之乎 ; 春秋無義戰 ; 不嗜殺人者能一之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: 4A.14: wars for land and cities fill fields and cities with the dead; this is leading the land to eat human flesh, a crime death cannot atone for, and the best fighters deserve the heaviest punishment. 6B.8: a humane man would not even take land from one state to give another; how much less seek it by killing people. 7B.2: in the Spring and Autumn period there were no righteous wars. 1A.6: only one who takes no pleasure in killing people can unite the realm.
rows.bearing: War context (rule 5). By analogy supports K0's 'gain' clause and K3: killing people for territory is condemned. Mencius still accepts punitive wars by a humane ruler (1B.8, 3B.5).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi (Li Lou I, Gaozi II, Jin Xin II, Liang Hui Wang I).

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.8 (ctext: Liang Hui Wang II, 8; Legge I.B.8)
rows.original: 聞誅一夫紂矣，未聞弒君也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked whether a subject may kill his ruler, as when Tang banished Jie and King Wu attacked Zhou, Mencius says one who ruins humaneness and rightness is a mere 'fellow'; he has heard of the punishing of the fellow Zhou, not of the murder of a ruler.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5, exclusions (a) and (b)): a campaign by a ruler against a tyrant. Counter-evidence considered; it gives no private person a licence to kill, so it does not decide.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.3 (ctext: Liang Hui Wang II, 3; Legge I.B.3)
rows.original: 夫撫劍疾視曰『彼惡敢當我哉』，此匹夫之勇，敵一人者也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius tells King Xuan not to love small courage: gripping a sword with a fierce look and saying 'How dare he face me?' is the courage of a common man, a match for one person. King Wen and King Wu, by one burst of anger, gave peace to all the people.
rows.bearing: K0: Implied; it ranks a private man's sword-drawing anger low rather than forbidding it. The kings' anger is war (rule 5); the passage approves righteous anger in a ruler, not in a private person.
rows.strength: Implied (K0); n/a for the war part
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: search budget exhausted; recalled from memory. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-ii.

rows.original: 孥戮汝
rows.translation: James Legge, SBE vol. 3 (1879), paraphrased
rows.says: In two battle oaths the king warns troops who disobey that he will punish them together with their children; commentators differ on whether this means death, enslavement or disgrace.

rows.reference: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xi 22nd year (638 BCE), battle of the Hong river; Gongyang Zhuan on the same year
rows.original: 君子不重傷，不禽二毛
rows.translation: No translation used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Duke Xiang of Song, refusing to attack the Chu army before it had formed up, said a noble person does not wound a man twice nor take the grey-haired captive. The Zuo Zhuan, which records the saying, reports his minister Ziyu calling it folly; the Gongyang praises the duke's conduct of the battle.
rows.bearing: K3 context only: a classical restraint on harming the wounded and the old in battle, and evidence that it was disputed. Not counted (rule 1).

rows.branch: All historical branches held the Book of Rites as a classic (Cheng-Zhu included); not counted under corpus.md
rows.reference: Book of Rites (Liji), Qu Li I (Summary of the Rules of Propriety, part 1)
rows.original: 父之讎，弗與共戴天；兄弟之讎，不反兵；交遊之讎，不同國
rows.translation: James Legge, SBE vol. 27 (1885), not displayed in this run; paraphrased
rows.says: One should not live under the same sky as the killer of one's father; against the killer of a brother one does not go home for a weapon; one does not live in the same state as the killer of a friend.
rows.bearing: Approves private revenge killing of a parent's killer. If counted, it would make K1 and K0 Contradicted (rule 2), or Unclear (rule 6) if read with the Rites of Zhou as a regulated, partly judicial practice. Not counted (rule 1), so reported beside the label; the labels depend on the Five Classics staying uncounted.

rows.original: 父不受誅，子復讎可也；父受誅，子復讎，推刃之道也
rows.translation: No translation used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese

rows.branch: Historical; read across later Confucian scholarship

rows.original: 駁復讎議 ; 復讎狀
rows.translation: No translation used; paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Chen Zi'ang had proposed executing an avenger under the law and then honouring him. rows.bearing: The tradition's own reconciliation of the Five Classics' approval of revenge with the rule that only officers may kill (Mencius 2B.8): revenge narrowed to unjust killings without redress and placed under the court. Later authorities (METHOD decision 7); outside the corpus; never decide.

support.reconciliation: Confucianism has no council or body with power to issue binding rulings, so its reconciliation comes from the counted texts themselves and from classical commentators and later scholars. (1) Counted texts (Tier 1, all branches): Mencius 7A.33 and 2A.2 state that killing even one innocent person is against humaneness and that the sages would not do it to gain the whole realm. Mencius 2B.8 teaches that even a murderer may be put to death only by the appointed judge, so no one acting on their own authority may kill, whatever the victim has done. Mencius 7A.35 keeps this even for the ruler's father: the judge must arrest him, and the son's love finds its outlet only by giving up the throne and fleeing, not by excusing the killing (Zhu Xi reads it this way, as law not bending for the ruler's kin; recalled, not verified). Analects 14.34 ('repay injury with uprightness') is glossed by Zhu Xi's Collected Commentaries (examination standard 1313 to 1905) as impartial fairness, not revenge. The Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 (Tier 2, treated as primary) places not repaying unreasonable treatment among the noble person's ways, and Mencius 5A.3 shows the model ruler Shun refusing revenge on a brother who tried to kill him. No counted text was found that permits a private killing. (2) Uncounted classics (Tier 2 or outside the corpus, canonical for all historical branches): the Book of Rites (Qu Li I; Tan Gong I, in Confucius's own words) approves a son's revenge on his parent's killer; the Gongyang Zhuan (Ding 4) allows it only when the father was killed unjustly; the Rites of Zhou places it under officers, by registering it with the judge and forbidding revenge on one who killed rightly. (3) The tradition's own way of joining these: later authorities read the classics' approval of revenge narrowly. Liu Zongyuan's Refutation of the Proposal on Revenge held revenge right only for an unjust killing that no court redressed; Han Yu's Memorial on Revenge (811) asked that every case go to the court for deliberation. Imperial codes punished private revenge, though lightly (Ming and Qing: sixty blows, none if done on the spot); these are outside the corpus and unverified here. Han Confucian voices and edicts (Dong Zhongshu; Emperor Guangwu, 35 CE, citing the Classic of Filial Piety) removed masters' power to kill slaves; these were verified by search in earlier project research. Mencius 7B.3 shows a further method of the tradition's own: Mencius refuses to believe a classic's report of mass killing because it conflicts with humaneness. Standing: counted texts decide; Zhu Xi and the older commentaries are classical authorities used for reconciliation; Liu Zongyuan, Han Yu and the codes are later authorities that never outweigh a counted text (METHOD decision 7). Here no counted text has to be outweighed; the tension is between counted texts and uncounted classics.

K1.label: Taught (provisional: the Explicit rows are UNVERIFIED in this run)
K1.reason: Counted Tier 1 texts teach K1: Mencius 7A.33 and 2A.2 (Explicit: killing even one innocent person is against humaneness), Mencius 2B.8 (Clear teaching: even a murderer may be killed only by the judge, never on private authority), and 7B.31 (wider rule, rule 7). These rows could not be verified in this run because the search budget was gone, so under rule 1 they do not yet decide. On verified evidence alone, the label rests on the Golden Rule as a wider rule reaching everyone: Analects 15.24 and 12.2 and the Great Learning ch. 10 (rule 7), verified by search in earlier project research and accepted in the same way for L1 in Article I's households annex. No counted text found permits a private killing. Mencius 7A.35 limits enforcement only, and Mencius 7B.7 presupposes revenge without approving it (rule 4). Caveat: the Book of Rites (Qu Li I; Tan Gong I, in Confucius's words) and the Gongyang Zhuan, canonical for every historical branch but Tier 2 and not counted, approve a son's revenge killing of his parent's killer. If they were counted, K1 would be Contradicted (rule 2), or Unclear (rule 6) if read with the Rites of Zhou's registration rule. So the label depends on the Five Classics staying uncounted, the same corpus question the households annex flagged.

K0.label: Taught (provisional: most rows UNVERIFIED in this run)
K0.reason: Gain: Mencius 2A.2 (Explicit: not one innocent killed even to win the realm), 5B.4 (Clear teaching: those who kill to seize goods are hated by all) and 3B.5 (Clear teaching: killing a child for his food). Anger: Analects 16.7 and 16.10 and 12.21 (Clear teaching, wider rule). Revenge: Mencius 2B.8 (only the judge may kill even a murderer), Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 (the noble person does not repay unreasonable treatment; treated as primary) and Mencius 5A.3 (Shun takes no revenge on a would-be murderer), all Clear teaching. The verified wider-rule rows (Analects 15.24 and 12.2; Great Learning ch. 10) also cover K0, since K0 is narrower than K1. All the specific rows are UNVERIFIED here and must be checked. The revenge clause is exactly where the uncounted Book of Rites and Gongyang Zhuan differ (they approve revenge for a parent), so K0 too depends on the Five Classics staying uncounted.

K3.label: Taught (record only; provisional, every counted row UNVERIFIED in this run)
K3.reason: Mencius 1B.11 condemns killing the fathers and elder brothers, and capturing the young, of a conquered people, and tells the king to send back the old and the young. Mencius 7B.4 has King Wu tell the enemy's people that he is not their enemy, and 7B.3 rejects a classic's report of mass bloodshed because a humane war would not cause it. All are Clear teaching for K3, and 4A.14 and 6B.8 condemn killing people for territory. Mencius still accepts punitive wars by humane rulers (1B.8, 3B.5), but never approves killing non-combatants in them. Uncounted context: the Documents' battle oaths threaten disobedient troops with punishment of their children (verified in earlier research, own troops, not enemies), and the Zuo Zhuan's 'do not take the grey-haired captive' (unverified). Until 1B.11 and 7B.4 are verified, no label is decided under rule 1.

rows.reference: Mencius 7B.7 (ctext Jin Xin II 7; Legge VII.B.7)
rows.original: 殺人之父，人亦殺其父；殺人之兄，人亦殺其兄
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius says he now knows how grave it is to kill a man's kin. If you kill a man's father, he will kill yours. If you kill his elder brother, he will kill yours. You do not kill your own father or brother yourself, but you are only one step away from it.
rows.bearing: Treats revenge killing by kin as something that will happen, and uses it to warn people off killing. It does not say that the avenger acts rightly. Rule 4: it presupposes a practice, so it is Implied and does not decide K1 or K0. Zhu Xi's commentary (unverified) says such a killing is really no different from harming one's own parents.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: the shared web search budget was exhausted before any search ran. Reference and wording are given from knowledge of the text. Check at ctext.org/mengzi/jin-xin-ii.

rows.reference: Mencius 7A.35 (ctext Jin Xin I 35; Legge VII.A.35)
rows.original: 執之而已矣……竊負而逃，遵海濱而處
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Tao Ying asks what would happen if Shun were emperor, Gao Yao his judge, and Shun's father Gusou killed a man. Mencius says Gao Yao would simply arrest him, and Shun could not forbid it, because Gao Yao's charge came from a proper source. Shun would throw away the empire like a worn sandal. He would secretly carry his father on his back, flee to the seashore and live there happily, forgetting the empire.
rows.bearing: Court context (a). It does not approve the killing. The killer is arrested even though he is the emperor's father, so the victim's protection does not depend on the killer's rank, which tells against grading protection by status. It limits a son's duty to bring a father who has killed to justice. That is a limit on enforcement, not permission to kill. Zhu Xi (unverified) reads it as the judge knowing only the law and the son knowing only his father, each acting rightly in his role. Xie Liangzuo, quoted by Zhu Xi on Analects 13.18, cites this story; that was seen in earlier project research.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: the search budget was exhausted. Its content is indirectly confirmed by the Zhu Xi and Xie Liangzuo comment on Analects 13.18, which earlier project research verified on ctext, but the passage itself was not checked.

rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: The Duke of She boasts of a man so upright that he gave evidence against his father for stealing a sheep. Confucius says that among his own people uprightness is different: a father covers for his son and a son for his father.
rows.bearing: Court context. It is about informing on kin for a theft, not about killing. It limits enforcement within the family, not the protection of life. No bearing on the labels.

rows.reference: Analects 14.34 (ctext Xian Wen 34; Legge XIV.36)
rows.original: 以直報怨，以德報德

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.2 (ctext Gong Sun Chou I 2; Legge II.A.2), the passage on Beigong You's courage
rows.original: 視刺萬乘之君，若刺褐夫……惡聲至，必反之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Among kinds of courage, Mencius describes Beigong You, who would stab a great prince as readily as a poor man and always returned an insult. Mencius ranks Meng Shishe's fearlessness above him. Above both he ranks Zengzi's courage of looking within: if I am in the wrong, I fear even a poor man; if I am in the right, I go forward against thousands.
rows.bearing: Describes a revenge-prone, assassin-like courage without approving it, and ranks it lowest. Rule 4: Implied, so it does not decide. Zhu Xi (unverified) calls Beigong You 'of the assassin type' (刺客之流).

rows.reference: Mencius 5A.3 (ctext Wan Zhang I 3; Legge V.A.3)
rows.original: 仁人之於弟也，不藏怒焉，不宿怨焉，親愛之而已矣
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Wan Zhang objects that Shun punished four great criminals but gave a fief to his brother Xiang, who spent every day plotting to kill him: 'others he punished, his brother he enfeoffed'. Mencius answers that a humane man does not store up anger or nurse resentment against his brother, but simply loves him. Shun also had officers govern the fief, so that Xiang could not oppress its people.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching against revenge, even against a would-be murderer (here a brother). A ruler's leniency to kin is a grading of punishment, which is court and ruler context (a), not a permission to kill. The text itself records the objection that this is partial.

rows.reference: Mencius 7A.33 (ctext Jin Xin I 33; Legge VII.A.33)
rows.original: 殺一無罪非仁也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Asked what a scholar's business is, Mencius says it is humaneness and rightness and nothing else. To kill one person who has done no wrong is against humaneness. To take what is not yours is against rightness.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Explicit that killing anyone without guilt is wrong. It sets no limit by status, faith or community (rule 7). With Mencius 3A.5 (an infant is without fault), it reaches newborns (rule 9). It does not say who may kill the guilty; Mencius 2B.8 answers that. Because it is unverified in this run, under rule 1 it cannot yet decide the label.

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.2 (ctext Gong Sun Chou I 2; Legge II.A.2)
rows.original: 行一不義、殺一不辜而得天下，皆不為也

rows.reference: Mencius 2B.8 (ctext Gong Sun Chou II 8; Legge II.B.8)
rows.original: 孰可以殺之？……為士師，則可以殺之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Shen Tong asked Mencius privately whether Yan might be attacked. Mencius said yes, and Qi attacked it. Mencius explains that if he had been asked who may attack it, he would have said only a 'minister of Heaven' (天吏). In the same way, if asked whether a man who has killed someone may be killed, he would say yes. If asked who may kill him, he would say the chief criminal judge (士師).
rows.bearing: K1 (private authority): Clear teaching that even a killer may be put to death only by the officer of justice, not by anyone who wishes. This answers the revenge duty in the uncounted Book of Rites. The killing it allows is judicial, which is context (a) under rule 5. K0: it rules out revenge on private authority. Mencius uses it to say that Qi, being no better than Yan, had no standing to attack (war context).

rows.reference: Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), ch. 10 in Zhu Xi's division (Legge ch. X)
rows.original: 寬柔以教，不報無道，南方之強也，君子居之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861), paraphrased
rows.says: Answering Zilu on strength, Confucius contrasts two kinds. The strength of the south is to be broad and gentle in teaching and not to repay unreasonable conduct, and the gentleman abides in it. The strength of the north is to sleep on weapons and armour and die without regret, and the merely forceful abide in that. Zhu Xi (unverified) glosses 不報無道 as accepting wrongs that come to one without retaliating.
rows.bearing: K0 (revenge): Clear teaching that the gentleman does not retaliate for wrongs. It is general, not about killing as such, and does not mention a parent's killer, so on its own it does not settle the Book of Rites' revenge duty. It supports K1.

rows.reference: Analects 12.21 (ctext Yan Yuan 21; Legge XII.21); see also 16.7 (Legge XVI.7)
rows.original: 一朝之忿，忘其身，以及其親，非惑與？
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: Confucius tells Fan Chi that it is delusion to let one morning's anger make you forget yourself and bring harm on your parents. In 16.7 he says that in the prime of life, when the blood is strong, the gentleman guards against fighting (戒之在鬥).
rows.bearing: K0 (anger): Clear teaching against violence driven by anger, though it does not name killing. It reasons from the harm that follows to oneself and one's family. Zhu Xi (unverified) reads it as checking anger.

rows.reference: Analects 12.10 (ctext Yan Yuan 10; Legge XII.10)
rows.original: 愛之欲其生，惡之欲其死……是惑也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: Confucius says it is delusion to want a person to live when you love them and to die when you hate them, and so to want both.
rows.bearing: K0 (hatred): Clear teaching against even wishing someone dead out of hatred. It is only Implied for the act of killing. Zhu Xi (unverified) adds that life and death are fated and not ours to wish for.

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.6 (Legge II.A.6) and Mencius 3A.5 (Legge III.A.5)
rows.original: 乍見孺子將入於井，皆有怵惕惻隱之心；赤子匍匐將入井，非赤子之罪也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity. A person without this feeling is not human, and it is the beginning of humaneness (2A.6). In 3A.5, Mencius notes that when an infant crawls towards a well, it is not the infant's fault.
rows.bearing: From birth onwards (rule 9): Clear teaching that infants are without fault and that care for them is the root of humaneness, so Mencius 7A.33 (do not kill the guiltless) reaches them. No counted text permits killing a newborn or a child. Taken alone, this is only Implied as a rule against infanticide.

rows.reference: Mencius 1A.4 (ctext Liang Hui Wang I 4; Legge I.A.4)
rows.original: 始作俑者，其無後乎！為其象人而用之也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius gets King Hui of Liang to agree that there is no difference between killing a man with a stick, with a sword or by bad government. He quotes Confucius: whoever first made tomb figures deserves to have no descendants, because they made images of people and used them in burials. How much worse, then, to let people starve to death.
rows.bearing: Implied against burying living people with the dead, the form in which masters' dependants were killed: Confucius condemns even the figurines. It also says that killing by policy is still killing (ruler context). Zhu Xi (unverified) explains that the figures looked too much like people.

rows.reference: Analects 13.19 (ctext Zi Lu 19; Legge XIII.19)
rows.original: 雖之夷狄，不可棄也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: Asked about humaneness, Confucius says: be respectful in private life, careful in your work and loyal to others. Even if you go among the Yi and Di peoples, these may not be set aside.
rows.bearing: Against limiting moral duties to one's own community: the same conduct is owed among foreign peoples. It is only Implied for K1, since it does not mention killing. No counted text found limits the protection of life to Chinese people or to Confucians.

rows.reference: Analects 10.17 in ctext and modern numbering (Legge X.12)
rows.original: 廄焚。子退朝，曰：「傷人乎？」不問馬
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: When the stables burned, Confucius came back from court and asked whether anyone was hurt. He did not ask about the horses.
rows.bearing: Implied for K1: concern for people of low status (in context probably stable workers) comes before property. It does not mention killing. It tells against grading protection by status.

rows.reference: Analects 14.21 in ctext numbering, not confirmed (Legge XIV.22)
rows.original: 陳恆弒其君，請討之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: When Chen Heng (Chen Chengzi) murdered Duke Jian of Qi, Confucius bathed, went to court and asked Duke Ai of Lu to punish him. Told to report to the three chief families, he did so, and they refused.
rows.bearing: Even for the murder of a ruler, Confucius does not act on his own authority but asks those with authority to act. This supports the private-authority part of K1 by example. It is Implied as a rule, and sits in ruler and war context (a, b). Zhu Xi (unverified) quotes Cheng Yi that Confucius would have proclaimed the crime and acted through the Son of Heaven and the lords.

rows.reference: Mencius 3B.9 (ctext Teng Wen Gong II 9; Legge III.B.9)
rows.original: 能言距楊墨者，聖人之徒也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius lists the Duke of Zhou's deeds: helping King Wu punish the tyrant Zhou, destroying fifty states and driving off wild beasts. He quotes an ode: 'the Rong and Di he smote'. He opposes the teachings of Yang Zhu and Mozi, and says that whoever can oppose them in words is a follower of the sages.
rows.bearing: Heterodox teachers are to be opposed by argument (言距), not harmed, so there is no permission for a zealot to kill (Implied support for K1). The wars against peoples called barbarian are war context (b). They are Implied, and do not teach killing people who are not fighting.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.8 (ctext Liang Hui Wang II 8; Legge I.B.8)
rows.original: 聞誅一夫紂矣，未聞弒君也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: King Xuan of Qi asks whether a minister may kill his ruler, citing Tang's banishing of Jie and King Wu's attack on Zhou. Mencius says that one who outrages humaneness is a robber, one who outrages rightness is a ruffian, and such a person is a mere 'fellow'. He has heard of the punishment of the fellow Zhou, but not of the killing of a ruler.
rows.bearing: Declares the killing of a tyrant to be punishment, not murder, because of what the victim did. This is war and ruler context (b, a): Tang and Wu were rulers leading armies. The tradition's own reading does not make it a licence for private assassination. Zhu Xi quotes Wang Mian (unverified): it holds only when those below have the humaneness of Tang and Wu and the one above has the cruelty of Jie and Zhou; otherwise it is usurpation and regicide. Compare Mencius 7A.31 (removing a ruler is right only with Yi Yin's purpose, otherwise it is usurpation) and 2B.8 (only a 'minister of Heaven' may attack). No bearing on the K1 label.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.7 (ctext Liang Hui Wang II 7; Legge I.B.7)
rows.original: 國人皆曰可殺，然後察之；見可殺焉，然後殺之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius tells the king not to put anyone to death because his attendants or his great officers say so. Only when all the people of the state say so should he examine the case, and only if he finds the person deserves death should he execute him. So it can be said that the people of the state put him to death.
rows.bearing: Court context (a). It does not license a crowd to kill: the ruler alone executes, after examining the case. It limits a ruler's killing.

rows.reference: Mencius 5B.4 (ctext Wan Zhang II 4; Legge V.B.4)
rows.original: 殺越人于貨……是不待教而誅者也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Quoting the Announcement to Kang in the Book of Documents, on those who kill people to rob them, do not fear death and are hated by everyone, Mencius says such people are to be executed without waiting for instruction. Each dynasty received this law.
rows.bearing: Court context (a). It concerns the ruler's law. It is not a private licence to kill robbers.

rows.reference: Analects 12.19 (ctext Yan Yuan 19; Legge XII.19)
rows.original: 子為政，焉用殺？
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: Ji Kangzi asks whether he should kill the lawless for the sake of the law-abiding. Confucius answers: in governing, why use killing? Desire what is good and the people will be good.
rows.bearing: Court context (a). It discourages even a ruler's killing of wrongdoers. No bearing on the labels.

rows.reference: Analects 20.2 (ctext Yao Yue 2; Legge XX.2)
rows.original: 不教而殺謂之虐
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), paraphrased
rows.says: Among the four evils of government, to put people to death without first teaching them is cruelty.
rows.bearing: Court context (a). It limits a ruler's killing. No bearing on the labels.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.5 (ctext Liang Hui Wang II 5; Legge I.B.5)
rows.original: 罪人不孥
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Under King Wen's government, punishing an offender did not extend to his wife and children. Zhu Xi glosses that hatred of wrongdoing stops at the offender himself.
rows.bearing: Court context. Children are not punished for their parents' crimes. This is the counted rule against the battle oaths of the Book of Documents, and it supports the equal protection of children.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.11 (ctext Liang Hui Wang II 11; Legge I.B.11)
rows.original: 若殺其父兄，係累其子弟……反其旄倪
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: After Qi took Yan, Mencius tells King Xuan that the people of Yan welcomed his army hoping to be rescued. If instead he kills their fathers and elder brothers, binds their sons and younger brothers, destroys their ancestral temples and carries off their treasures, how can that be right? He should quickly send back the old and the young, stop removing the treasures, set up a ruler with the people's agreement, and withdraw.
rows.bearing: K3: Clear teaching that a conquering army must not kill or carry off the conquered population, and must send back the old and young it has taken. Protection reaches an enemy state's people. War context, so it does not decide K1.

rows.reference: Mencius 3B.5 (ctext Teng Wen Gong II 5; Legge III.B.5)
rows.original: 有童子以黍肉餉，殺而奪之……為匹夫匹婦復讎也……誅其君，弔其民
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Tang sent his people to plough for the chief of Ge. The chief robbed those bringing food and killed those who resisted, including a boy carrying millet and meat. Tang attacked Ge because of the boy, and everyone said he did it not for wealth but to avenge common men and women. In his campaigns he punished rulers and comforted their peoples, who welcomed him like rain in a drought.
rows.bearing: Condemns killing a child for gain (Clear teaching for K0, and for K1 for children). K3: a rightful campaign is aimed at the ruler and spares the people. It also approves a war framed as revenge for commoners, but that is war context (b), not private revenge.

rows.reference: Mencius 7B.3 (ctext Jin Xin II 3; Legge VII.B.3)
rows.original: 以至仁伐至不仁，而何其血之流杵也？
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius says it would be better to have no Book of Documents than to believe all of it. Of the 'Completion of the War' chapter he accepts only two or three slips. When the most humane attacks the most inhumane, how could the blood have flowed until it floated the pestles?
rows.bearing: K3: the tradition's own way of reading an ancient war record of mass slaughter is to doubt it, because the humane do not slaughter. Clear teaching, in war context. Zhu Xi (unverified) says Mencius feared that later readers would be misled and their cruelty encouraged.

rows.reference: Mencius 4A.14 (ctext Li Lou I 14; Legge IV.A.14); see also 7B.2 and 7B.4
rows.original: 爭地以戰，殺人盈野……故善戰者服上刑
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Wars fought for land fill the fields with the dead, and wars fought for cities fill the cities. This is leading the land to eat human flesh, a crime that death is not enough to atone for. So those skilled at war should suffer the heaviest punishment. In 7B.2 Mencius says that in the Spring and Autumn period there were no righteous wars, and in 7B.4 that saying 'I am good at battle' is a great crime.
rows.bearing: War context (b). It condemns wars of gain and the killing they bring. It supports K3 in spirit, though it does not single out people who are not fighting.

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.3 (ctext Liang Hui Wang II 3; Legge I.B.3)
rows.original: 此匹夫之勇，敵一人者也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), paraphrased
rows.says: Mencius asks King Xuan not to love small courage. Gripping a sword, glaring and saying 'who dares face me?' is the courage of a common man, a match for one opponent. King Wen and King Wu, by one burst of anger, gave peace to all the people.
rows.bearing: Private angry violence is called petty (K0, Implied). A ruler's anger that leads to a just war is approved, but that is war context (b).

rows.branch: Canonical for every historical school; not counted under corpus.md and METHOD.md section 9, decision 4
rows.reference: Book of Rites (Liji), Qu Li I 曲禮上 (Legge, SBE vol. 27)
rows.original: 父之讎，弗與共戴天；兄弟之讎，不反兵；交遊之讎，不同國
rows.translation: James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 27 (1885), paraphrased
rows.says: One does not live under the same sky as the man who killed one's father. Against the man who killed one's brother, one does not go home to fetch a weapon. One does not live in the same state as the man who killed one's friend. Legge adds in brackets that one should seek to kill him.
rows.bearing: Approves revenge killing by a son or brother on his own authority. If counted, it would contradict K1 and K0 for one class of victim, a parent's killer (rules 2 and 5). It is not counted, so it is reported beside the label (rule 1). It is the strongest counter-evidence in the Confucian canon.

rows.branch: Canonical for every historical school; not counted (decision 4)
rows.reference: Book of Rites (Liji), Tan Gong I 檀弓上, Zixia's question on avenging parents (Legge, SBE vol. 27)
rows.original: 寢苫枕干，不仕，弗與共天下也；遇諸市朝，不反兵而鬭
rows.translation: James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 27 (1885), paraphrased
rows.says: Zixia asks Confucius how to live while the killer of one's parents lives. Confucius says: sleep on straw with your shield as a pillow, take no office, do not share the world with him, and if you meet him in the market or at court, fight him at once without going home for a weapon. For a brother's killer: do not serve in the same state, and if you are on the ruler's mission, do not fight him even if you meet him. For a cousin's killer: do not lead, but if the chief avenger can act, follow behind him with a weapon.
rows.bearing: Attributed to Confucius, it commands private revenge for parents and brothers. If counted, it would contradict K1 and K0 (rules 2 and 5). It also ranks the ruler's service above revenge for a brother. Not counted (rule 1).

rows.reference: Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), Offices of Earth (Diguan), the Mediator 調人; and Offices of Autumn (Qiuguan), the Officer of the Court 朝士
rows.original: 凡殺人而義者，不同國，令勿讎，讎之則死……凡報仇讎者，書於士，殺之無罪
rows.translation: No public-domain English (Édouard Biot's French, 1851); paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: The Mediator settles feuds. The killer must move beyond the seas from a father's avenger, a thousand li away from a brother's, and out of the state from a cousin's. Avenging a killing that was righteous is forbidden on pain of death. In quarrels, whoever strikes first is punished. The Officer of the Court rule says that whoever takes revenge after registering it with the judicial officer kills without guilt.
rows.bearing: It regulates and limits revenge, but also lets a registered avenger kill without guilt. Whether that killing is judicial or private is disputed, so if counted it would make K1 Unclear (rule 6) or contradicted. Not counted.

rows.reference: Gongyang Commentary (Gongyang zhuan), Duke Yin 11th year
rows.original: 君弒，臣不討賊，非臣也；子不復讎，非子也
rows.translation: No public-domain English found; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Explaining why the Spring and Autumn Annals do not record the burial of a murdered ruler, Master Shen says: if the ruler is murdered and his ministers do not punish the murderer, they are not ministers; if his son does not take revenge, he is not a son.

rows.branch: Canonical for the historical (New Text) school; not counted
rows.reference: Gongyang Commentary, Duke Ding 4th year (Wu Zixu) and Duke Zhuang 4th year (Duke Xiang of Qi)
rows.original: 父不受誅，子復讎可也；父受誅，子復讎，推刃之道也……家亦可乎？曰：不可
rows.translation: No public-domain English found; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: On Wu Zixu: if a father was killed without being guilty, his son may take revenge. If the father was justly executed, revenge only starts an endless exchange of blades, and revenge does not reach the killer's son. On Duke Xiang of Qi avenging an ancestor nine generations back: a state may do so even after a hundred generations, but a family may not.
rows.bearing: Permits a son's revenge for an unjust killing, which would contradict K1 and K0 if counted. It also limits revenge: never for a lawful execution, never against the killer's descendants, and for a family never across generations. Not counted. Wu Zixu's revenge was taken through a war (b).

rows.original: 禮不下庶人，刑不上大夫
rows.translation: James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 27 (1885), paraphrased

rows.reference: Book of Rites (Liji), Tan Gong II 檀弓下: Chen Ganxi's maidservants; and Chen Zikang on his brother Chen Ziju's burial
rows.original: 以殉葬，非禮也
rows.translation: James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 27 (1885), paraphrased
rows.says: Chen Ganxi, dying, ordered that his two maidservants be put in his coffin with him. His son refused, saying that burying people with the dead is against ritual, still more so in the same coffin, and they were not killed. In a second story, Chen Zikang stops his dead brother's wife and steward from burying people with him for the same reason, saying that if anyone should go it is the two of them.
rows.bearing: Uncounted support against a master killing his servants at his death, and against obeying a dying master's order to do so. Not counted (rule 1).

rows.reference: Xunzi, ch. 28, Youzuo 宥坐; the same story is in the Kongzi Jiayu (Shi Zhu 始誅) and the Shiji (Kongzi shijia), both outside the corpus
rows.original: 孔子為魯攝相，朝七日而誅少正卯
rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Seven days after becoming acting chief minister of Lu, Confucius had Shaozheng Mao, a well-known man, put to death. Asked why, he names five evils worse than theft, among them a mind that is clever but dangerous, conduct that is perverse but stubborn, and speech that is false but persuasive.

If its judicial character were disputed it would be a hard case (rule 6), but Xunzi is not counted. rows.original: 笑君者罪當死
rows.translation: No public-domain English found; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: At the meeting at Jiagu, Qi had a jester dance in mockery by the Lu ruler's tent. Confucius said that mocking a ruler deserves death and had the marshal carry out the law. The man was executed.

rows.branch: Canonical for every historical school; not counted
rows.reference: Book of Documents (Shangshu), Speech at Gan 甘誓 and Speech of Tang 湯誓

rows.translation: James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 3 (1879), paraphrased

rows.original: 小棰則待過，大杖則逃走……殺天子之民，其罪奚若？
rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Zeng Shen damages a melon root, and his father beats him senseless with a big stick. Confucius rebukes Zeng Shen for submitting. Shun waited out a small rod but ran from a big stick, so that his father never committed the crime of a bad father. A son who lets his father kill him in anger leads his father into wrongdoing, and Confucius asks: are you not a subject of the Son of Heaven, and what is the crime of killing a subject of the Son of Heaven?
rows.bearing: The tradition's own story treats a father killing his son in anger as a crime, and the son's submission to it as unfilial. Outside the corpus, so reported beside the label.

rows.original: 旌與誅莫得而並焉
rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Chen Zi'ang had proposed executing Xu Yuanqing, who killed the official who had killed his father, and then honouring him. Liu answers that one cannot both execute and honour the same act. If the father was killed unjustly, out of private spite, the son's revenge keeps the rites and should not be punished; he cites the Gongyang Commentary and the Rites of Zhou. If the father was lawfully executed, revenge is defiance of the ruler's law and must be punished.
rows.bearing: A classical authority, outside the corpus, who accepts revenge for an unlawful killing. It shows that the wider tradition did not simply reject revenge. It would cut against K1 and K0 if it were counted.

counter.reconciliation:
Confucianism has no living body with authority to rule for the tradition, and no living branches that count different texts. Its reconciliation therefore lies in its counted texts and its classical commentators.

(1) Counted texts: the Four Books, which have the highest standing. The Mencius says that killing one person without guilt is against humaneness (7A.33), and that the sages would not kill one innocent person even to gain the empire (2A.2). Asked who may kill someone who has killed, Mencius answers: the criminal judge (2B.8). The Doctrine of the Mean names not retaliating for wrongs as the gentleman's strength (ch. 10). The Analects calls violence from one morning's anger delusion (12.21), and calls wishing death on those one hates delusion too (12.10). In the Mencius, revenge appears only as a fact used to warn people off killing (7B.7). Where filial love and justice meet, the texts let a son cover for a father (Analects 13.18) or flee with him (Mencius 7A.35). Even so, the judge still arrests the emperor's father: these texts limit enforcement, not the victim's protection. Mencius 1B.8 (the tyrant as a mere 'fellow') belongs to rulers and war, and Mencius himself narrows it in 7A.31 and 2B.8.

(2) Classical commentators: Tier 2, with high standing. Zhu Xi's Collected Commentaries on the Four Books were the examination standard from 1313 to 1905. Zhao Qi's commentary on the Mencius and He Yan and Xing Bing's Lunyu zhushu are the older standard. Earlier project research verified that Zhu Xi reads the 'straightness' of Analects 14.34 as impartiality without private feeling, not retaliation. The following were not verified in this run. Zhu Xi reads 7B.7 as showing that killing another man's father is no different from harming one's own. He restricts 1B.8 through Wang Mian's comment: it holds only for a Tang or a Wu against a Jie or a Zhou, and otherwise it is usurpation and regicide. He glosses 'not repaying the unreasonable' (Doctrine of the Mean 10) as accepting wrongs without retaliating.

(3) The wider classical canon: Tier 2. It is not counted under decision 4, but every historical school held it canonical, and it was primary for Han to Tang classical learning. The Book of Rites (Qu Li I; Tan Gong I, where the teaching is attributed to Confucius), the Rites of Zhou and the Gongyang Commentary make avenging a father a duty. They already limit it: no revenge for a lawful execution and none against the killer's son (Gongyang, Duke Ding 4); no revenge across generations for a family (Duke Zhuang 4); and in the Rites of Zhou, mediation, exile of the killer, death for avenging a righteous killing, and registration with the judge. The counted texts never cite these revenge passages, and Mencius 2B.8 gives the killing of a killer to the judge. But no counted text expressly rejects the revenge duty either. This is the main unresolved tension, and only the corpus decision keeps it out of the label.

(4) Later authorities: outside the corpus, with the standing of classical writers and of state law. Chen Zi'ang (around the 690s) proposed executing an avenger and then honouring him. Liu Zongyuan answered that revenge is right against an unlawful killing but is defiance of the ruler when the killing was a lawful execution. Han Yu (811) said that the classics and the law conflict here and that each case should go to the throne. Imperial codes forbade private revenge but punished it lightly, and the Ming and Qing codes excused some private killings. The Tang Code graded the protection of slaves and of disobedient children. In 1394 the Ming emperor and Ministry of Rites refused to honour the killing of a child in the name of filial piety, against the Guo Ju model of popular literature. In the Kongzi Jiayu, Confucius treats a father killing his son in anger as a crime.

(5) Modern: there is no authorised body. Modern scholars have debated Mencius 7A.35 and Analects 13.18 (a debate on concealing kin in China, about 2002 to 2004, unverified), but they have no standing to rule for the tradition.

K1.label: Taught (provisional: the deciding counted rows are UNVERIFIED in this run, and on verified counted texts alone the label would be Silent)
K1.reason: Mencius 7A.33 (killing one guiltless person is against humaneness) and 2A.2 (the sages would not kill one innocent person even for the empire) are Explicit and set no limit by status, faith or community (rule 7). Mencius 2B.8 is Clear teaching that even a killer may be put to death only by the criminal judge, so private persons may not kill even the guilty. Mencius 3A.5 and 2A.6 show that infants are without fault and that care for them is the root of humaneness (rule 9). No counted text was found that permits a master, parent, husband, kinsman, crowd, zealot or religious leader to kill. Mencius 7B.7 only presupposes revenge (rule 4, Implied). Mencius 7A.35 and Analects 13.18 limit enforcement within the family and fall under court context (rule 5). Mencius 1B.8 is ruler and war context. The result depends on the Five Classics staying uncounted (decision 4). If the Book of Rites were counted, Qu Li I and Tan Gong I, which command a son to kill his father's killer, would make K1 Contradicted (rules 2 and 5). The Rites of Zhou rule on registered revenge would at least make it Unclear (rule 6).

K0.label: Taught (provisional, for the same reason as K1)
K0.reason: Gain: Mencius 2A.2 is Explicit, and Mencius 3B.5 condemns killing a boy for his food. Revenge: Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 (the gentleman does not repay the unreasonable, Clear teaching), Mencius 5A.3 (no stored anger or nursed resentment even towards a would-be murderer) and Mencius 2B.8 (killing a killer belongs to the judge). Anger: Analects 12.21 and 16.7. Hatred: Analects 12.10, Implied. Analects 14.34 (repay injury with straightness, not kindness) is a limit, not a permission: Zhu Xi reads straightness as impartiality. The uncounted Book of Rites, Rites of Zhou and Gongyang Commentary command or allow revenge for a father, exactly what K0 forbids. They are reported beside the label and would contradict K0 if counted.

K3.label: Taught (Clear teaching, provisional; 'those who have surrendered' not addressed in the counted texts found)
K3.reason: Mencius 1B.11 condemns a conquering army that kills the fathers and elder brothers of the conquered and carries off their sons, and tells the king to send back the old and the young. Mencius 3B.5 has a rightful campaign punish the ruler and comfort the people. Mencius 7B.3 refuses to believe a record of mass slaughter by the humane. Mencius 4A.14, 7B.2 and 7B.4 condemn wars of gain. Against this, Mencius 3B.9 (the Duke of Zhou destroying fifty states and smiting the Rong and Di) is Implied only. The uncounted battle oaths of the Book of Documents threaten soldiers' children. The uncounted Spring and Autumn commentaries are divided on Duke Xiang of Song's rule sparing the wounded and the grey-haired. Context only, as the brief requires.

Calling the offender a beast is not a licence to harm him: the point is that he is not worth contending with. Unverified, so it does not decide (rule 1).
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule, wrongs to oneself)

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.6 (ctext Gong Sun Chou I, 6; Legge II.A.6) and 3A.5 (ctext Teng Wen Gong I, 5; Legge III.A.5)
rows.original: 乍見孺子將入於井，皆有怵惕惻隱之心 ; 赤子匍匐將入井，非赤子之罪也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: 2A.6: anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, not for gain or praise; whoever lacks this heart is not human, and it is the beginning of humaneness. 3A.5: in a debate with the Mohist Yi Zhi about whether love should be graded, Mencius remarks that when an infant crawls towards a well it is not the infant's fault.

Reading 3A.5 as 'infants are without fault, so 7A.33 reaches them' is the researcher's inference; 7A.33 reaches newborns by its own plain words in any case.

rows.reference: Mencius 5B.4 (ctext Wan Zhang II, 4; Legge V.B.4), quoting the Announcement to Kang (Kang Gao) of the Classic of Documents
rows.original: 殺越人于貨，閔不畏死，凡民罔不譈 … 是不待教而誅者也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked whether one may accept gifts from a man who robs travellers outside the city gate, Mencius says no, and quotes the Documents: those who kill people to seize their goods, reckless and unafraid of death, are hated by all the people. Such men are put to death without waiting to teach them; each dynasty received this law.
rows.bearing: K0 (gain): Clear teaching, through an approved quotation, that killing people for their goods is among the gravest wrongs. The execution of such killers is court context (rule 5), not a private licence to kill robbers. Does not decide until verified (rule 1).

rows.reference: Mencius 3B.5 (ctext Teng Wen Gong II, 5; Legge III.B.5)
rows.original: 有童子以黍肉餉，殺而奪之 … 為匹夫匹婦復讎也
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: The chief of Ge robbed those bringing food to the fields and killed those who would not hand it over, among them a boy carrying millet and meat. King Tang attacked Ge because of that boy, and all said he did it not to enrich himself but to avenge ordinary men and women. His campaigns punished rulers and comforted their peoples.
rows.bearing: K0 (gain) and K1 (children): Clear teaching, through an approved story, that killing even a child to take his food is a grave wrong. Tang's 'revenge' is a punitive war by a ruler (rule 5, exclusion (b)), not private revenge. K3: a rightful campaign is aimed at the ruler and spares the people. Does not decide until verified (rule 1).

rows.reference: Mencius 5A.2 and 5A.3 (ctext Wan Zhang I, 2 and 3; Legge V.A.2 and V.A.3)
rows.original: 仁人之於弟也，不藏怒焉，不宿怨焉，親愛之而已矣
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Shun's father and his half-brother Xiang tried to kill him (burning the granary he was repairing, filling in the well he was digging). Wan Zhang objects that Shun as ruler punished four great criminals but gave Xiang a fief. Mencius answers that a humane man does not store up anger or nurse resentment against his brother; he simply loves him. Shun had officers govern the fief so that Xiang could not oppress its people.
rows.bearing: K0 (revenge): Clear teaching, through the model ruler, that one takes no revenge even on someone who tried to kill you. Its stated reason concerns a brother, so on its own it reaches kin only. A ruler's leniency to kin is a grading of punishment (court and ruler context, rule 5), not a permission to kill. Does not decide until verified (rule 1).

rows.reference: Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 10 (Zhu Xi's division; Legge ch. X; Zhong Yong chapter of the Book of Rites)
rows.original: 寬柔以教，不報無道，南方之強也，君子居之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked by Zilu about strength, Confucius contrasts the strength of the south (teaching with breadth and gentleness, not repaying unreasonable conduct), in which the noble person abides, with the strength of the north (sleeping on weapons and armour, dying without regret), in which the forceful abide; he then urges a strength that holds to harmony and the mean.

Zhu Xi is recalled as glossing it as taking outrage without retaliating (not verified). Not used to decide K0 even when verified, because the same Book of Rites contains revenge passages that are excluded (see fairness notes).

rows.original: 一朝之忿，忘其身，以及其親，非惑與 ; 血氣方剛，戒之在鬥 ; 忿思難，見得思義
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), not displayed; paraphrased

rows.original: 能言距楊墨者，聖人之徒也 ; 歸，斯受之而已矣
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased

rows.translation: James Legge, SBE vol. 27 (1885), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Zixia asks Confucius how to live while the killer of one's parents lives. rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese

rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese

rows.reference: Analects 14.34 (ctext Xian Wen 34; Legge XIV.36)
rows.original: 以德報怨，何如？…以直報怨，以德報德
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked about repaying injury with kindness, Confucius asks what would then repay kindness: repay injury with straightness, and kindness with kindness.
rows.bearing: Limits a duty to forgive or return good for evil; it is not permission to kill. rows.reference: Mencius 7A.35 (ctext Jin Xin I, 35; Legge VII.A.35)
rows.original: 執之而已矣 … 竊負而逃，遵海濱而處
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked what would happen if Shun's father killed a man while Shun ruled and Gao Yao was judge, Mencius says Gao Yao would simply arrest him, and Shun could not forbid it. Shun would throw away the realm like an old sandal, carry his father off in secret and live happily by the sea.
rows.bearing: Limits a son's part in enforcing the law against his father, not the victim's protection: the killing is a crime even for the ruler's father, and the arrest is right. Court context (rule 5). Does not contradict K1 or K0.

rows.original: 凡有復父讎者，事發，具其事申尚書省
rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese

rows.reference: Liu Zongyuan, Refutation of the Proposal on Revenge (駁復讎議), answering Chen Zi'ang on the case of Xu Yuanqing
rows.original: 旌與誅莫得而並焉
rows.translation: No public-domain English used; paraphrased by the project from the Chinese
rows.says: Chen Zi'ang had proposed executing Xu Yuanqing, who killed the official who had killed his father, and then honouring him. Liu answers that one cannot both execute and honour the same act. If the father was killed unjustly, out of private spite, the son's revenge keeps the rites and should not be punished (citing the Gongyang and the Rites of Zhou); if the father was lawfully executed, revenge defies the ruler's law and must be punished.
rows.bearing: Narrows revenge to unjust killings, but still accepts it there, so it cuts against K1 and K0 for that class if it were counted. It shows the wider tradition did not simply reject revenge. Outside the corpus; never decides (rule 1).

rows.reference: Mencius 1B.7 (ctext Liang Hui Wang II, 7; Legge I.B.7) and 4B.4 (ctext Li Lou II, 4; Legge IV.B.4)
rows.original: 國人皆曰可殺，然後察之；見可殺焉，然後殺之 ; 無罪而殺士，則大夫可以去
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1895), not displayed; paraphrased

verified.reconciliation:
Confucianism has no living body with authority to rule for the tradition. Its reconciliation therefore lies in its counted texts, its classical commentators and later scholars. Under METHOD decision 7, later authorities never outweigh a counted text.

(1) Counted texts (the Four Books). Verified: the Analects (15.24, 12.2) and the Doctrine of the Mean (ch. 13) give the rule 'do not impose on others what you would not want yourself'. The Great Learning (commentary ch. 10) applies it to anyone with power over others. Zhu Xi's gloss 推己及物 (verified in Article I research) extends it to everyone. Not verified in this run, but bearing directly: Mencius 7A.33 and 2A.2 (killing even one innocent person is against humaneness, and the sages would not do it to gain the realm), and Mencius 2B.8 (only the criminal judge may put even a killer to death). The Mencius mentions revenge only as a warning against killing (7B.7). Where filial love meets justice, Analects 13.18 (verified) lets a son cover for a father, and Mencius 7A.35 has Shun flee with his father, yet the judge still arrests the ruler's father. Xie Liangzuo, quoted by Zhu Xi on 13.18 (verified), reads this as the law still standing. Analects 14.34 asks that injury be repaid with 'straightness', which Zhu Xi glosses as complete impartiality without private feeling (confirmed in earlier research; number not displayed). No counted text was found that permits a private killing.

(2) The wider classical canon. It is Tier 2 and not counted (decision 4), but every historical school held it canonical, and it was primary for Han to Tang learning. The Book of Rites (Qu Li I; Tan Gong I, in Confucius's own words, wording verified through a Taiping Yulan quotation) makes avenging a parent a duty. The Gongyang (Ding 4, verified) allows revenge only when the father died unjustly, and calls revenge for a lawful execution 'pushing the blade back and forth'. The Rites of Zhou puts revenge under officers: mediation, exile of the killer, death for avenging a righteous killing, and registration with the judge. These texts already narrow revenge. The counted Mencius never cites them and gives the killing of a killer to the judge (2B.8), but no counted text expressly rejects the revenge duty. That is the main unresolved tension, and only decision 4 keeps it out of the label.

(3) Later authorities, outside the corpus and none verified in this run unless noted. Han Yu (811) asked that every revenge case go to the court. Liu Zongyuan held revenge right against an unlawful killing and a crime against a lawful one. Imperial codes punished private revenge lightly or, in the Ming and Qing, not at all when done on the spot. The Tang Code graded the protection of slaves and of disobedient children. Han Confucian voices and Emperor Guangwu's edict of 35 CE removed masters' power to kill slaves, citing the Classic of Filial Piety ch. 9 (verified). Song officials such as Su Shi campaigned against drowning newborns, and in 1394 the Ming Ministry of Rites refused to honour killing a child in the name of filial piety, against the Guo Ju model of popular literature. The Kongzi Jiayu (verified in part) treats a father killing his son in anger as a crime.

(4) Net: the tradition's own movement is to narrow revenge and place it under the court, not to reject it outright in the wider canon. In the counted Four Books, killing even the guilty belongs only to the judge.

The Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 (the noble person does not repay unreasonable conduct) is recorded but deliberately not used to decide. Other chapters of the same Book of Rites approve revenge and are excluded, and using one chapter while excluding the others would tilt the result.

Analects 14.34 ('repay injury with straightness') limits a duty to forgive; it is not a permission. Zhu Xi reads straightness as complete impartiality (confirmed in earlier research).

The revenge clause is exactly where the uncounted canon differs. The Book of Rites commands revenge, and the Gongyang (Ding 4, verified earlier) and the Rites of Zhou allow a son's revenge for a parent killed unjustly. Counted, they would make K0 Contradicted (Book of Rites) or at least Unclear (Rites of Zhou). The same three dependencies as K1 apply.

verified.branch_notes:
Confucianism has no living branches that count different texts (decision 4). The Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools and modern New Confucians all hold the Four Books, so every counted row speaks for all of them. The Lu-Wang school uses the older text order of the Great Learning, but the passage used is in both orders.

Han to Tang classical learning, for which the Five Classics (with the Gongyang and the Rites of Zhou) were primary, is a historical school, not a living branch. Its revenge texts are therefore reported beside the label. The Qing New Text (Gongyang) revival is likewise historical.

Xunzi is contested: Neo-Confucian orthodoxy rejected him, and some modern Confucians value him. He is never sole evidence, and his Shaozheng Mao story is court context in any case.

Not checked:
- Korean and Japanese Confucian schools and law (for example the Japanese debate over the revenge of the forty-seven ronin, 1703);
- modern Confucian religious bodies;
- modern New Confucian statements on killing.

If a modern body or school were found that counts the whole Book of Rites as primary, rule 3 would apply to it: Contradicted in one branch, through Tan Gong I.
verified.fairness_notes:
1. One book, two standards. The Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean are chapters of the Book of Rites and count as primary, while its Qu Li and Tan Gong chapters, which approve revenge, do not. Earlier independent checks flagged this tilt. To avoid it:
- K1 and K0 are decided here only by the Tier 1 Analects rows.
- The Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 (do not repay unreasonable conduct) is recorded but not used to decide K0's revenge clause.
A reader who thinks the whole Book of Rites should count would see K1 and K0 Contradicted. The same standard must then apply to any tradition whose wider canon commands private revenge, for example the avenger of blood in Numbers 35:19.

2. The wider-rule route. Confucianism's verified result rests on the Golden Rule read as a wider rule that reaches killing. If the project lead rejects that reading, the rejection must apply to every tradition whose result rests on a Golden Rule. Equally, Confucianism should not be held to a stricter test than traditions whose general 'harm no one' clauses were accepted (secular humanism in this run; Sikhism, Taoism and Digambara Jainism in Article I).

3. Verification failure is environmental. Mencius 7A.33 and 2A.2 are among the best-known lines in the canon. That they do not count here reflects the exhausted search budget and the unreachable reference site, not the tradition. An adherent would rightly object if the article reported Confucian support as weaker than that of traditions whose sites could be searched.

4. State law and popular literature. The Tang, Ming and Qing codes, the Guo Ju story and the Mingshi case are not texts of the tradition's teaching. They are listed for transparency only. Listing imperial law as 'counter' must not be read as Confucian teaching. The same practice should be followed for every tradition, either listing comparable state law and popular literature or listing none.

5. Wrong attributions avoided. The Han Feizi's report of parents killing newborn daughters is Legalist, not Confucian, and is rightly excluded.

6. Teaching style. Confucian texts teach through sayings, dialogues and stories. The Clear teaching ratings for Mencius 2B.8 (an analogy) and 5A.3 (a story about the model ruler) match how the project rates parables elsewhere, and should not be lowered because of style.

7. Hard texts shown in full. The revenge passages, including the one in Confucius's own mouth, are shown, and so is the tradition's own narrowing of revenge (Gongyang, Rites of Zhou, Han Yu, Liu Zongyuan). An adherent should recognise both as fair.
